summary: Before any rover, instrument or astronaut goes to Mars or the Moon, it must be tested on Earth, in places that partially reproduce those conditions. Finding the right analog for each test is slow and scattered across papers. We built Planet Analog Search, an open-source web platform that ranks Earth sites by their similarity to a planetary target. A researcher picks a Mars, Moon or volcanic preset (or types 8 environmental and soil parameters, or uploads a surface image), and the engine ranks 1,000 sites in under one second using a weighted, normalized Euclidean distance, with thermal amplitude weighted highest. Results appear on an interactive map, in a side-by-side comparison matrix, and in a scientific console that builds the NASA POWER API query for the selected site. We start with Pampas de La Joya (“Mar de Cuarzo”), Arequipa, Peru: a hyper-arid, oxidizing, low-organic soil studied with NASA Ames as a Mars analog, and a site now threatened by mining and land invasions. Our goal is to help researchers choose sites with data before traveling, and to give this unique Peruvian analog a scientific purpose that supports its protection.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Planet Analog Search is a web platform that finds Earth analogs for planetary targets. Users can (1) choose a Mars, Moon or volcanic preset, (2) enter 8 parameters (max/min temperature, atmospheric pressure, solar radiation, UV index, labile organic carbon, soil friction and cohesion), or (3) drag and drop a surface image so a vision model fills in the parameters. One click ranks 1,000 sites by similarity.

HOW IT WORKS

The engine computes 7 features (thermal amplitude = Tmax − Tmin, pressure, solar radiation, UV, organic carbon, friction, cohesion), normalizes them with Min-Max over the whole corpus, and ranks sites with a weighted Euclidean distance (score = 1/(1+d)). Weights: thermal amplitude 3.0, pressure 2.0, solar radiation 1.5, UV 1.5, organic carbon 1.0, friction 1.0, cohesion 0.5. Results are shown on a Leaflet map (all sites, top-5 matches, selected winner), a comparison matrix (target vs. site), and a scientific console that generates the NASA POWER API query for the selected site.

CURRENT STATUS (honest)

This is a working prototype. The dataset contains 4 reference analogs (Pampas de La Joya, Altiplano – Laguna Salinas, Valle de los Volcanes de Andagua, Yungay) plus 996 demo sites. The vision model is currently simulated through a swappable adapter (Clean Architecture). Next steps: load NASA POWER, MODIS, ASTER and SMAP values for every site and connect the NASA–IBM geospatial foundation model.

WHY PAMPAS DE LA JOYA

"Mar de Cuarzo" (16.74°S, 72.04°W, 1,154 m) is the northern tip of the Atacama Desert. Peer-reviewed studies with NASA Ames scientists report hyper-aridity (only 4 small rain events in 4 years, all during El Niño), ~20% soil humidity, high oxidant activity, and less organic matter than Yungay. Microbes survive under quartz rocks and in evaporites, making it valuable for life-detection research. Its soil was used in NASA–CIP "Potatoes on Mars". The site is threatened by mining exploration and land invasions.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Researchers, space agencies, engineering teams and universities can screen analog sites with data before funding fieldwork, saving time, money and risk. For Peru, it gives a unique site a scientific purpose that supports its protection.

SMART ROADMAP

3 months: real NASA data for every site and the vision model live. 6 months: present the evidence to Peruvian research groups and authorities. 12 months: first pilot field campaign with a Peruvian university or agency.

TOOLS

Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn; React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React-Leaflet; Esri/OpenStreetMap basemaps; NASA POWER API; GitHub.

CREATIVITY

It turns scattered analog research into a searchable, visual "search engine for other worlds", with multimodal input (parameters or images) and a direct bridge to NASA data for every result.
